readerTitle: Why an investor backs the loss-maker over the profitable shop
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주방용품 매장 체인, 온라인 도매 플랫폼, 라멘 가게, 10개 투자 포트폴리오) + 벤처 수익 분포에 관한 실제 연구는 일반적으로만 서술
insight: 벤처 투자자는 '이 회사가 망하지 않을까'가 아니라 '잘되면 얼마나 커질 수 있나'를 묻는다. 소수의 큰 성공이 나머지 손실을 모두 메우기 때문이다.
misconception: 투자자는 가장 안전하고 이미 이익을 내는 사업을 좋아한다. 모든 투자자는 같은 기준으로 사업을 본다.

sources.text: 벤처캐피털 수익 분포 연구: 소수의 거래가 전체 수익의 대부분을 만든다는 분석 (예: Horsley Bridge 펀드 데이터를 인용한 Benedict Evans, 'In praise of failure', 2016; Correlation Ventures 분석)
포트폴리오, 라멘 가게, 매장 체인 수치는 모두 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 5번 카드는 연구 결과를 구체적 수치 없이 일반적으로만 서술했습니다. 수치를 넣으려면 원자료를 확인하세요. 흔히 인용되는 값: Horsley Bridge 1985~2014 데이터에서 약 6%의 거래가 수익의 약 60%를 만들었다는 내용, 그리고 거래의 절반가량이 원금 이하로 끝났다는 내용.
3번 카드 계산: $10M 펀드, $1M씩 10곳. 5곳 × $0 = $0, 3곳 × $1M = $3M, 1곳 × $3M = $3M, 1곳 × $20M = $20M. 합계 $26M = 2.6배. 가장 큰 성공을 빼면 $6M으로 원금 $10M보다 적음(손실). 가상 수치이며 수수료·기간은 단순화를 위해 제외.
8번 카드의 '연 20% 안팎의 꾸준한 수익'은 설명용 가정입니다. 특정 국가의 대출·투자 제도에 관한 조언으로 읽히지 않도록 일반적인 표현만 썼습니다.

cards.title: Why an investor backs the loss-maker over the profitable shop
body: Two founders pitch the same investor on the same morning. One runs four profitable kitchenware stores. The other runs an online wholesale platform that loses money every month.
The investor backs the platform. She isn't being reckless. She's doing math the store owner never saw.

image.label: Two founders waiting outside an investor's office
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 대기실 의자에 두 창업자가 앉아 있음. 한 사람은 냄비·주걱이 담긴 상자를 들고 있고 그래프는 완만한 상승, 다른 사람은 노트북을 들고 있고 그래프는 아래로 꺾였다가 가파르게 치솟는 점선. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: You have $1M to invest from a venture fund.
body: Pitch one: four kitchenware stores, profitable, growing about 10% a year. Very likely to be around in ten years.
Pitch two: an online platform where small shops order stock from wholesalers. Losing money. Maybe a 1-in-10 chance it becomes huge. Which fits your fund?

options.text: The kitchenware stores. Safe and already profitable
options.feedback: You'd likely get your money back with a modest gain. But a fund full of modest gains rarely covers its many failures.

options.text: The wholesale platform, if the huge outcome is believable
options.feedback: You accept likely failure in exchange for a small chance of a result big enough to pay for many losses. The next card shows why.
It feels balanced, but half your money now sits where it can't move the fund's results much, and the platform gets less fuel.

cards.title: One winner pays for nine.
body: A $10M fund puts $1M into each of ten companies. Total back: **$26M**, or 2.6 times the money. Remove the single biggest winner and the fund gets back $6M. It loses money.

cards.title: Investors think in portfolios, not single bets
body: Venture investors know most of their bets will disappoint. Their results come from a **power law**: a few outliers earn more than all the others combined.
So the key question isn't "Will this survive?" It's "If this works, could it be big enough to matter to my whole fund?" A safe business that can only double rarely passes that test.

image.label: Ten bars, one towering over the rest
image.brief: 막대 10개 인포그래픽. 9개는 바닥에 붙거나 낮고, 1개만 화면 위까지 치솟음. 위에 "Could this one return the fund?" 문구. 단순하고 깔끔한 색.

cards.softwareNote: Software often fits this pattern because one more customer costs little to serve. That's why venture money crowds into software, and why investors ask about market size so early.

cards.title: The data looks lopsided.
body: Studies of venture fund records keep finding the same shape. Many deals lose money or just return it. A small share of deals produces most of the gains.

This explains behavior that looks odd from outside. Investors may pass on a solid company, back a strange idea, or push founders to grow faster than feels comfortable. They're hunting for the rare outlier, because missing it costs more than losing on a few failures.

cards.title: A lender thinks the opposite way.
body: A bank lender or a cautious local backer doesn't share in a huge win. They get their money back plus interest, at best.
So they care about downside: steady cash, assets, a record of paying bills. To them, the profitable kitchenware stores are the better deal, and the money-losing platform is too risky.
Same business, opposite verdicts. Before you pitch, work out **which logic** the person across the table uses.

cards.title: Venture money comes with venture goals.
body: If you take money from someone hunting outliers, you sign up for their goals. Expect pressure to grow fast and aim big, even when slower growth would be safer for you.
Inflating your story to sound like an outlier doesn't help either. Investors test big claims against real evidence, like customers who come back.
And plenty of excellent businesses will never be venture-shaped. That says nothing about their quality. It just means a different kind of money fits them.

cards.title: Now it's a ramen shop.
body: Your ramen shop is busy and profitable. You want $300K to open a second location nearby. You expect it to earn steady returns, about 20% a year on the money, with little chance of becoming a national giant.

options.text: A venture fund, since they have the most money
options.feedback: A steady 20% a year can't pay for a fund's many failures. Expect a quick no, or pressure to become something you don't want to be.

options.text: A lender or local backers who value steady cash
options.feedback: Their logic matches your business: reliable returns, low downside. You give up the dream of a huge payout, which you weren't chasing anyway.

options.text: A venture fund, pitched as "the next 1,000-location chain"
options.feedback: It may get a meeting, but a claim you can't back with evidence usually falls apart. If it works, you've signed up for a growth race you didn't plan.

cards.title: Venture investors buy the chance of a huge outcome, not safety.
body: A few big wins pay for many losses, so they ask how big you could get. Lenders ask how safe you are. Pitch to the logic of the money you want.
**Try it today:** write one sentence on how big your business could realistically get. Then decide which kind of investor that sentence would excite.
